A shared genomic locus or operon correspondence across the source and reference strains has not been established; retain a candidate rather than assuming equivalent CRISPR complexes.

Retain A0A7E6FSU6 as the primary Swiss-Prot accession. The four returned oxidase-family hits have only about 25-27% global identity and incomplete query coverage. They do not establish a D-aspartate oxidase counterpart; a D-amino-acid oxidase-like label is not evidence of matching substrate specificity. No supported counterpart was identified by this search.

Retain A2AXI2 as the primary Swiss-Prot accession. The only hit is the related RlmN methyltransferase A0A2T4Q1F7 (33.69% global identity), not an established Cfr counterpart. Shared radical-SAM/RNA-methyltransferase ancestry does not establish the Cfr resistance activity or gene identity. The source is strain 11562A; no supported reference-strain counterpart was identified.

Retain A6Q0K5 as the primary Swiss-Prot accession. All 107 residues of the Swiss-Prot protein align identically to the 131-residue reference protein, which has a 24-residue extension. Both records share RefSeq XP_001694345.2, supporting the counterpart assignment independently of the sequence match. The precursor boundary difference is explicit; the sequences are not literally identical.

Retain A9PCL4 as the primary Swiss-Prot accession. B9ILP9 at POPTR_018G083500 is the manually assessed reference-proteome counterpart: 161/162 identical residues, full ungapped coverage, and only N117D. The competing POPTR_001G423500 paralog (A0A2K2CCD0) differs at seven residues. The original EF146010 cDNA is explicitly from Nisqually-1, so a different cultivar cannot explain this pair. This is a sequence-supported locus assignment, not a shared primary-record locus cross-reference; the one-residue discrepancy remains unexplained.

Retain B5UBC1 as the primary Swiss-Prot accession. The leading hit is reviewed PIK5-NP, with the synonym PIKM1, but only 58.42% global identity and extensive differences. The source cultivars differ, and the reference record describes Nipponbare lacking AVR-Pik recognition. A related resistance-locus representation is plausible, but copy-number, locus and specificity differences prevent an equivalence assertion.

Retain D2KBH9 as the primary Swiss-Prot accession. The 418-residue reference protein differs by one residue across full ungapped coverage (99.76% identity), with a large separation from other metallopeptidase hits. This supports a qualified sequence-based counterpart assessment. The source protein is from strain Breton; the origin and biological effect of the single residue difference are not established.

Retain F7J0M4 as the primary Swiss-Prot accession. Both reviewed records represent RGA4 in different rice cultivars, and the reference entry is the leading full-length match. UniProt contrasts AVR-Pia recognition in Aichi asahi/Sasanishiki with its absence in Nipponbare. Record this as a reference-cultivar locus counterpart, not equivalent resistance function; loss of recognition by the RGA4/RGA5 system does not establish that RGA4 alone is inactive.

Retain F7J0N2 as the primary Swiss-Prot accession. Q2R8L1 is a plausible reference-proteome counterpart, but the captured evidence does not independently map the Sasanishiki protein to the Nipponbare locus. The target is named RGA5 at Os11g0225300 / LOC_Os11g11810; those identifiers locate the target only. The sequence is substantially divergent (624 identities over 1105 paired residues, with 207 gap columns), and the cultivar-dependent AVR-Pia recognition statement concerns the resistance system. Retain a candidate pending cross-cultivar locus mapping; do not assert equivalent receptor specificity or protein integrity.

Hybrid H11-11 provenance and the absence of a direct locus cross-reference leave allele, model, and paralog alternatives unresolved. Mapping source genomic record U01661, including flanks, to the reference assembly is needed before promoting this relationship.
